title: Fats & Oils
subtitle: 1750–1850 · Candles, Lamps and Soap: Spermaceti and the Golden Age of American Whaling, Argand and Gas, Chevreul’s Chemistry and the Palm Oil of “Legitimate Commerce”

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Abolition and the oil trade; the soap excise

entries.label: The English soap excise: a tax that leaves a record
entries.hint: Britain taxed soap by excise until 1853, so its consumption can be counted: per capita use more than doubled from 3.1 pounds in 1791 to 8 pounds in the 1860s, somewhat above France’s, with unknown quantities smuggled from France and Ireland to evade the levy. Proposals for a soap duty were printed as early as 1707, and the soap-makers’ own ‘case’ against it in 1711.
entries.note: SECONDARY (two scholarly works read): Ward, The Clean Body (2019), section ‘The art of soap making’ (excise, per capita figures, repeal in 1853); Lowengard, ‘On the Disappearance of the Animal Body’, Historical Studies in the Natural Sciences 53(3) (2023) pp.242–255, notes citing the 1707 Proposals … for Laying a Small Duty upon Soap and The Case of the Soap-Makers Making Green Soap (1711). The start date of the excise is not given in the passages read, so the date range starts at the 1711 pamphlet.

entries.label: Britain abolishes the slave trade; the oil trade fills its place
entries.loc: London and the Bight of Biafra
entries.hint: After Britain’s abolition of the slave trade in 1807 the Bight of Biafra ports that had shipped slaves turned to palm oil, ‘legitimate commerce’, though Law warns the label is Eurocentric — palm oil had been exported before abolition, from the 1790s — and that the slave trade itself remained ‘legitimate’ in African eyes. In oil a great canoe carried about nine tons, so a trader needed nine times as many canoes to match the return on a slave cargo.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly book read): Law, From Slave Trade to ‘Legitimate’ Commerce (1995) Introduction pp.1–11 (PDF pp.38, 73; the canoe arithmetic at p.11, PDF p.23) and Lynn, Commerce and Economic Change in West Africa (1997) pp.1–3, 18. The 1807 date is the date of the British Act; Law gives imports of palm oil to Britain from the 1790s.

entries.label: Russia’s Lenten loophole: the sunflower is not on the list of forbidden oils
entries.hint: Heiser writes in Kiple that the sunflower reached Europe in the sixteenth century but was not an early success as a food until it reached Russia. The Russian Orthodox Church kept very strict dietary rules during the 40 days of Lent and during Advent, and in the early nineteenth century its list of prohibited foods covered nearly all those rich in oil; the sunflower, perhaps unknown to the church authorities, was not on the list, and the Russian people eagerly took up a seed that could be eaten while obeying the letter of the law. By the middle of the century Russia was the world’s leading producer of sunflower, oil from the seed was being extracted there from the early nineteenth century, and the stems were harvested for potash, some of it exported.
entries.note: SECONDARY (book read): Heiser, ‘Sunflower’, in Kiple & Ornelas, eds., The Cambridge World History of Food (2000), PDF p.465 (printed p.428), citing Gilmore (1931) and Putt (1978). ‘Perhaps unknown to the church authorities’ is the author’s conjecture, and the passage names no Lenten list or date more precise than the early nineteenth century. The bracket 1800–1850 is the folio’s. Compare fats-1500-1750::th2 and fats-1500-1750::b1.

entries.label: Cod liver oil becomes a medicine: iodine, trimethylamine and the search for the active principle
entries.loc: The cod-fishing countries of the North Atlantic, place not named
entries.hint: O’Keefe writes in Kiple that cod liver oil was reportedly used for medicine in the eighteenth century, long before vitamins were known, for bone afflictions, rheumatism, tuberculosis and, later, rickets. Cod has supplied more than 90 per cent of the volume of fish-liver oils, which also come from pollock, haddock, shark and halibut; cod livers hold 20 to 70 per cent fat, a range explained by the fish laying down fat before spawning and using it up during. In an account of 1895, F. P. Moller describes the hunt for the oil’s active ingredient: iodine, detected in it as far back as 1836, was followed by trimethylamine, so that herring brine briefly became the desideratum of the day, and then by the free fatty acids. Kiple says Moller wrongly concluded that there was no specific active principle, since the liver oils are rich in vitamins A and D.
entries.note: SECONDARY (book read, quoting Moller 1895): O’Keefe, ‘An Overview of Oils and Fats, with a Special Emphasis on Olive Oil’, in Kiple & Ornelas, eds., The Cambridge World History of Food (2000), PDF p.423 (printed pp.385–386). ‘Reportedly’ is Kiple’s word for the eighteenth-century medical use, and the passage names no country, physician or trade; the 1836 date is for the detection of iodine.

entries.label: Chevreul shows what a fat is
entries.hint: The French chemist Michel-Eugène Chevreul’s work on animal fats and soap, begun about 1812 and published in 1823 as Recherches chimiques sur les corps gras d’origine animale, provided the scientific understanding of saponification: fats are compounds of fatty acids with a base. It gave soap and candle manufacture a precision they had lacked and led to the stearin candle and the margarine of the next decades. A 1795 report by Darcet on soap was an earlier systematic inquiry.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly works read): Ward, The Clean Body (2019), ‘The art of soap making’ (research published 1813–1823); Lowengard (2023) pp.242–255 (begun about 1812, Recherches 1823; Darcet’s 1795 report); Aoyagi, History of Hydrogenation, Shortening and Margarine (PDF p.48, quoting Lewkowitsch 1903 that Chevreul ‘laid the scientific foundation’ of the fat industry). The stearin candle and margarine consequences are the folio’s links, not stated in these passages.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Spermaceti, 735 whaleships, palm oil tonnages, Marseille’s soap kettles

entries.label: Spermaceti candles: the brightest light, and a cartel to control the oil
entries.hint: About the middle of the 1700s the colonists learned to make candles from spermaceti, the waxy ‘head matter’ of the sperm whale, which burned with a brilliance, clarity and purity no other candle had. The craft became a foundation of colonial commerce, and on 5 November 1761 the eight largest candle manufacturers formed the ‘United Company of Spermaceti Chandlers’, the Spermaceti Trust, to fix a maximum price they would pay for head matter — a price rival buyers could simply outbid.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Dolin, Leviathan (2007; 2016 ed.) pp.125–126 (spermaceti as medicine and the candles), p.146 (‘the middle of the century … the colonists first made candles from spermaceti’) and pp.152–153 (the Trust of 5 November 1761).

entries.label: Soap consumption doubles
entries.hint: British per capita soap consumption more than doubled between 1791 and the 1860s, from 3.1 pounds to 8 pounds, and about three quarters of the soap made was for household use; French production averaged some 62,000 tons a year in the early nineteenth century by one account. British soap making clustered around the great ports — London, Liverpool, Bristol, Plymouth and Newcastle.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly book read): Ward, The Clean Body (2019), ‘The art of soap making’; Ward notes that the estimates ‘vary’ even for Britain and that the French figures are unclear.

entries.label: Walvis Bay: twenty to thirty Yankee whaleships a season by 1795
entries.loc: Walvis Bay, Saldanha Bay and Table Bay
entries.hint: When the American Revolution cut Britain off from New England whale oil, whalers began to use the southern African coast: Saldanha, Angra Pequena and Walvis bays were favourites for right-whale shore whaling in the southern winter, and by 1795 twenty to thirty Yankee whaleships were anchoring in Walvis Bay every season. Yankee captains were said to choose such bleak places to make it harder for crews to desert. The African coast supplied the whales; the ships and the market were American and British.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis, Men and Whales (1991) p.126 (PDF p.149). The ‘to make it harder for crews to desert’ is a saying Ellis reports (‘it was said’), not a record.

entries.label: Imported oilseeds challenge olive oil in the soap kettle
entries.hint: Marseille soap, made from olive oil, was one of the great regional soaps, with Venice, Naples and Castile; at mid-nineteenth century the city had about 50 makers and some 700 workers. From the early years of the century, however, imported vegetable oils challenged the olive’s dominance and chemistry created new products, so that Marseille, though it kept the prestige of the true ‘savon de Marseille’, gradually lost its national predominance; by the later 1800s soap manufacture was widespread in France.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly book read): Ward, The Clean Body (2019), ‘The art of soap making’ (Marseille: about 50 manufacturers with some 700 workers; ‘imported vegetable oils had challenged the olive’s dominance’). Ward does not name the oils; Law and Lynn show palm oil, and the Unilever histories show copra and groundnut, entering later.

entries.label: Whaling is Tasmania’s first industry: the Derwent, 1804–1838
entries.hint: Ellis calls whaling Australia’s first industry: right whales were so thick in the Derwent estuary that fifty or sixty might be seen at once, and shore crews rowed out, harpooned and lanced them and towed them to tryworks on land, each whale yielding about 6 tuns of oil and 300 pounds of bone. By 1804 five ships had left New South Wales for England with sperm oil; in 1830 the Deveron sailed for London with 200 tons of oil and 20 tons of bone worth some £5,000. With no rules, rival crews fought over who had struck first, and once twenty-one boats chased one whale; a series of laws had been passed by 1838.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis, Men and Whales (1991) pp.101–104 (PDF pp.124–127); the 1804 and 1830 figures are his. The Derwent whalers are treated here as one case of the colonial bay-whaling that Ellis traces round Australia and New Zealand.

entries.label: Liverpool slave traders become palm-oil importers
entries.hint: Several Liverpool slave-trading houses turned to palm oil after abolition: the Tobins, George Case, Jonas Bold and James Penny among importers, and Charles Horsfall, founder of the largest palm-oil firm in Liverpool in the early nineteenth century, who had been deeply involved in the West Indian trade before 1807.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly book read): Law (1995) ch.3 (PDF p.75), citing the evidence on the Tobins, Case, Bold, Penny and Horsfall. The dates given are the span of the transition; individual firms’ dates are not in the passage.

entries.label: The golden age of American whaling: 735 ships
entries.loc: Nantucket, New Bedford and Sag Harbor
entries.hint: From the end of the War of 1812 to the late 1850s the American whaling industry went through ‘unparalleled growth, productivity and profits’: 25 ships sailed from Nantucket in 1815, 61 by 1819, and the whole American fleet peaked at 735 ships out of about 900 worldwide, the largest whaling fleet in history, sailing for sperm, right, bowhead, gray and humpback whales in every ocean. New Bedford passed Nantucket in the 1820s (288 ships to Nantucket’s 62 in 1850) and peaked at 329 ships in 1857, about half the American fleet. Dolin dates the peak to 1846 in one chapter and 1854 in another.
entries.note: ANCHOR (two books read): Dolin (2007; 2016 ed.) p.241 (PDF p.241; ‘peaked at 735 ships in 1846’) and the epilogue to the ‘Shipping List’ passage, p.393 (PDF p.393; ‘a high of 735 in 1854’) — an internal discrepancy in the book, not resolved here; Davis, Gallman & Gleiter, In Pursuit of Leviathan (1997) pp.242, 248, 252 (PDF; Nantucket 25 → 61 vessels 1815–1819; New Bedford 288 against Nantucket’s 62 in 1850, 329 at its 1857 peak; Sag Harbor’s peak in 1847).

entries.label: British palm-oil imports leap tenfold in a generation
entries.loc: Britain and the Bight of Biafra
entries.hint: Between 1815–20 and 1846–50 British palm-oil imports from West Africa rose from under 2,000 tons a year to over 22,000, and from £90,000 to £725,000 in value; prices reached a pre-1850 peak of £47–64 a ton in 1818–19, then fell to £23–27 in the 1820s. Old Calabar’s exports, 700–800 tons a year before 1807, reached 2,000 tons by 1820 and 4,000–5,000 by 1833, when total British imports were 13,345 tons.
entries.note: ANCHOR (statistical tables read): Law (1995) ch.2 p.47 (PDF p.59; Customs figures for 1815–20 and 1846–50, and the prices) and Lynn (1997) ch.1 p.18 (PDF p.38; Old Calabar, with her reference to CUST 5/16-34). The ‘tenfold’ in the label is the folio’s arithmetic on Law’s ‘less than 2,000’ and ‘over 22,000’.

entries.label: Honolulu and Lahaina become the whalers’ ports: six hundred arrivals in 1846
entries.hint: The Hawaiian islands, first visited by American whalemen in 1819, quickly became the foremost stopping-off point for whaleships in the Pacific; by the middle of the century the ports of Honolulu and Lahaina were hosting many hundreds of whaleships a year, reaching a high of six hundred arrivals in 1846. Captains used them to unload cargoes and ship them east, to stock up and to hire crew. The crews themselves, Dolin writes, were a polyglot mixture that included Pacific islanders, and a nineteenth-century observer said that a more heterogeneous group of men had never assembled in so small a space as in the forecastle of a New Bedford sperm whaler.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Dolin, Leviathan: The History of Whaling in America (2007), PDF pp.258 and 278–279. Islanders appear here as port hosts and crew, not as makers or users of oil; the Hawaiians’ own fats are not covered.

entries.label: Palm oil greases the railways and lights the towns
entries.hint: Palm oil was used as a lubricant for industrial machinery and railway rolling stock and was an essential ingredient in soap and candles; it was also a source of glycerine and used in processing tinplate. Hopkins sees the expansion of palm products and groundnuts as a response to industrial growth in Europe: soap for the growing towns, lubricants for the new machinery, above all the railways, and candles for lighting the towns and factories. Manufacturers urged the public to ‘buy our candles and help stop the slave trade’.
entries.note: SECONDARY (two scholarly books read): Lynn (1997) Introduction p.3 (PDF p.23; palm oil as lubricant, soap, candles, glycerine, tinplate) and Hopkins, An Economic History of West Africa (2020 ed.) PDF p.193, whose note 12 gives the slogan. The span is the early nineteenth-century boom the passages describe; the slogan is undated there.

entries.label: New Zealand’s shore whalers: as many as a hundred stations on Cook Strait
entries.loc: Cook Strait and the Bay of Islands, New Zealand
entries.hint: New Zealand’s bay and shore whalers hunted the right whale from stations, perhaps as many as a hundred, most of them on either shore of Cook Strait, with others at the Bay of Islands, the Banks and Otago peninsulas and Foveaux Strait; the stations were stinking piles of guts, bones and blubber. Maori, who knew whale meat and oil from stranded whales but had not gone whaling themselves, joined as ‘toungers’, crews who contracted to tow whales in exchange for the tongue. British, American and French ships worked the coast, the French from 1836, and the Treaty of Waitangi followed on 6 February 1840.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis, Men and Whales (1991) pp.114–116 and 124 (PDF pp.137–139, 147); the Nantucket whaler Mary Mitchell’s journal of 1836 is his source for the ‘toungers’. Ellis gives no start date for the shore stations, so the decade is the date of the sources he quotes. ‘As many as a hundred’ is his estimate.

entries.label: James Low’s coconut and nutmeg estates at Province Wellesley, 1830s
entries.hint: Lees writes that James Low, appointed Superintendent of the Prai area, then known as Province Wellesley, acquired title about 1832 to recently abandoned land parcels, several of which he turned into nutmeg plantations, and that he also owned large estates planted in coconuts and rice. Convicts sent from India provided cheap, unfree labour for roads and bridges, and a wave of enthusiastic planters produced spices, coconuts, indigo and tapioca for the regional and global market. Travellers of the 1830s, in her telling, insisted that British-ruled enclaves differed from Malay-governed states in their prospects for development.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Lees, Planting Empire: Cultivating Subjects in British Malaya, 1786–1941 (2017), ch.1, PDF pp.42–43, citing Low’s Penang settlement account. The passage is about plantation settlement, not oil; the coconut estates are the only fat crop in it.

entries.label: Bristol: soap city and palm-oil port
entries.hint: Bristol traders built an increasingly important palm-oil trade in the early nineteenth century, a position owed to the city’s role as a soap-making centre; in 1834, the first year with precise statistics, Bristol imported about 5,590 cwt of palm oil, around 2 per cent of the British total, and by 1850 53,656 cwt, 12 per cent. Its leading oil traders, the King family, like the Tobins of Liverpool, traced their mercantile origins to the slave-trade era.
entries.note: ANCHOR (statistics cited in a scholarly book): Lynn (1997) ch.2 p.28 (PDF p.48).

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The Argand lamp, gaslight and industrial soap

entries.label: Argand’s lamp: oil burns without smoke
entries.hint: In 1783 the chemist François Ami Argand unveiled in Paris an oil lamp with a hollow, tubular wick, a glass chimney and a mechanism for raising the wick, built on Lavoisier’s findings: its double air supply burned the soot that dimmed ordinary flames, and the chemist Macquer reported a white, lively, almost dazzling light with no smoke or smell. Schivelbusch calls it for the nineteenth-century household what the bulb was for the twentieth, yet it remained an improved oil lamp.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Schivelbusch, Disenchanted Night (1988) ch.1 pp.10–14 (PDF pp.12–14), citing Schroeder, The Argand Burner (1969) and Macquer’s report of 1783. The fuels used (colza and other oils) are not specified in the passage read.

entries.label: Steam, Leblanc soda and Chevreul turn soap making industrial
entries.hint: Three developments altered soap making fundamentally in the first half of the nineteenth century: steam power and mechanisation; Nicolas Leblanc’s late-eighteenth-century process for making alkali from salt, which reduced reliance on wood and plant ashes and brought large-scale caustic soda (more widely used in England than France); and Chevreul’s research of 1813–1823 on animal fatty acids and soap. Together they gave the capacity to manufacture soap on an unprecedented scale, and showed that soap’s future lay with industrial chemistry.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly book read): Ward, The Clean Body (2019), ‘The art of soap making’; the Leblanc date is Ward’s ‘late eighteenth century’ (the process is usually dated 1791).

entries.label: Gaslight: a light without a wick
entries.hint: In 1810 an MP asked the gas engineer William Murdoch before a Commons committee whether a light without a wick was possible. The standard manuals explained that the whole difference between a gasworks and a candle or lamp was to put the distillation at a distance, rather than in the wick, where oil, wax or tallow decomposed as fast as it burned: the first industrial challenger to fat-based light.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Schivelbusch (1988) ch.1 pp.14–15 (PDF p.14), citing Smiles, Lives of the Engineers p.349 and Clegg’s Practical Treatise on the Manufacture and Distribution of Coal-Gas (1841). Schivelbusch gives the comparison of brightness in ch.1 (PDF p.27: gas three times as bright as tallow candle on Accum’s figures).

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The Bight of Biafra; California’s olives

entries.label: Serra plants olives at San Diego; Jefferson admires them
entries.hint: In 1769 Fray Junípero Serra and his Franciscans introduced olives to North America with a grove at their mission on San Diego Bay, and founded twenty-one more missions along the California coast over the next half-century, each with olives of the cultivar known as ‘mission’. Thomas Jefferson saw olive trees on a muleback trip across the Alps in 1788, called them ‘the richest gift of heaven’, and tried to grow them at Monticello, but his cuttings would not take.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the chapter on the New World (Serra 1769, the 21 missions, Jefferson 1788); Kiple (2000) II.E.1 p.378 (Jefferson’s failed cuttings; California’s success by the early twentieth century).

entries.label: The Bight of Biafra becomes the world’s oil coast
entries.loc: Old Calabar, Bonny and the Cameroons
entries.hint: The ports of the Bight of Biafra led the oil export after 1807: Old Calabar first, then Bonny, which by the late 1840s overtook it, exporting some 7,000–8,000 tons of oil against Old Calabar’s 3,000–5,000; in 1855 the Bight’s ports shipped 25,060 tons (Elem Kalabari and Bonny 64 per cent, Old Calabar 16 per cent). Palm oil was also feeding the ships of the middle passage, so the trade was both the slave trade’s provisions and its replacement.
entries.note: ANCHOR (scholarly book read): Lynn (1997) ch.1 pp.18–21 (PDF pp.38, 39, 41; Table 1.5, from Hutchinson, Impressions of Western Africa, 1858). Bonny’s overtaking of Old Calabar is dated only loosely (1827–33 or after 1834) by Lynn.

entries.label: Groves, not plantations: how the oil was made in West Africa
entries.hint: The palm-oil trade of the nineteenth century grew from natural groves tended by local farmers — 200 to 300 palms to the hectare in the heart of the Niger Delta region, ‘the greatest grove area of Africa’ — with some deliberate planting in Dahomey and among the Krobo near Accra, though contemporary Europeans often called any farm with palms a ‘plantation’. In the 1840s Dahomey and the Niger Delta exported about 1,000 and 13,000 tonnes a year, rising to 5,000 and 20,000 by the 1880s.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly chapter): Kiple (2000) II.E.3 p.398 (PDF p.435), citing Hartley 1988, Manning 1982, Reid 1986 and Lynn 1989. The densities refer to the 1940s.

entries.label: The revolutionary wars end Dutch whaling
entries.hint: Dutch whaling, which in 1670 had sent 178 ships to Spitsbergen, declined sharply in the last two decades of the 1700s — twelve ships were trapped and crushed in the West Ice in 1777 — and collapsed completely during the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars of 1795–1804, leaving the northern whale oil trade to the British and then the Americans.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis, Men and Whales (1991) p.66 (PDF p.89); the handover to British and American whalers is the folio’s reading.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Slavery inside Africa under the oil boom

entries.label: Britain’s soap boom drives slavery inside West Africa
entries.hint: Law argues that growing British demand for soap and other oil-based commodities was an important stimulus to the use of slave labour within West Africa between 1820 and 1850, and perhaps earlier in places: the end of the Atlantic slave trade did not end slavery, since producing oil for export used enslaved labour inside Africa.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly argument): Law (1995) ch.3, p.51 (PDF p.63). It is Law’s thesis in the book, not an uncontested finding; Lynn and Hopkins engage the same question.
